card.title: Locking Down an API With Spring Security

a1.cap: Secure the API: /actuator/health and GET /api/public/ are open, /api/admin/ requires role ADMIN, everything else requires authentication. Use stateless HTTP Basic (no sessions, CSRF disabled for this pure API) and BCrypt-hashed passwords.

lines: Secure the API: /actuator/health and GET /api/public/ are open, /api/admin/ requires role ADMIN, everything else requires authentication. Use stateless HTTP Basic (no sessions, CSRF disabled for this pure API) and BCrypt-hashed passwords.

a1.cap: Modern Spring Security is configured with a SecurityFilterChain bean built by a lambda DSL. Authorization rules are matched top to bottom, so open endpoints come first and the catch-all comes last.
a1.say: Modern Spring Security is configured with a Security Filter Chain bean built by a lambda DSL. Authorization rules are matched top to bottom, so open endpoints come first and the catch-all comes last.

a1.cap: Stateless session management suits token or Basic auth for APIs; never store plain-text passwords, so expose a PasswordEncoder bean.
a1.say: Stateless session management suits token or Basic auth for APIs; never store plain-text passwords, so expose a Password Encoder bean.

a1.cap: One SecurityFilterChain bean defines how every request is secured.
a1.say: One Security Filter Chain bean defines how every request is secured.

a1.cap: CSRF protection matters for cookie-based browser sessions; a stateless API using headers can disable it.
Stateless means no HTTP session: every request must authenticate itself.
Health checks stay open so load balancers can probe the service.
Admin endpoints require the ADMIN role, otherwise 403 Forbidden.
The catch-all rule comes last: everything else needs a logged-in user, otherwise 401.
BCrypt hashes passwords with a salt and a tunable cost, so a stolen table is hard to crack.
